6.0.0.en: Multiplied: the number of Christians meant here is not specified, but the last figure St. Luke mentioned is five thousand (ch. 4:4), so the number must have been greater than that.

6.0.1.en: The disciples: a title given to Christians at that time because they were disciples of Christ and the Apostles, living a common life and all learning from the twelve Apostles.

6.0.2.en: Neglected: unintentionally, as a result of the large number and the Apostles' lack of time, so they forgot to distribute to some.

6.0.3.en: The daily ministration: the distribution of gifts was every day.

6.0.4.en: About 6 years after the founding of the Church, a problem emerged, which was the murmuring of the Jews of the Dispersion (who were abroad and had spoken Greek since the days of the Babylonian exile) against the Jews who had not left Jerusalem and spoke Hebrew, because the widows of the first group were not receiving enough of the daily distribution of material needs, and perhaps that made them feel like strangers, which increased their sensitivity.

6.1.0.en: The multitude of the disciples: the members of the Church in general, and especially those harmed by the poor and insufficient distribution.

6.1.1.en: It is not reason: that is, God does not accept and approve.

6.1.2.en: The word of God: preaching and teaching.

6.1.3.en: Serve tables: the distribution of gifts and material needs, called tables because the food is set on tables.

6.1.4.en: The conduct of the Apostle Fathers was exemplary, for they did not defend themselves or deny, but sought to solve the problem, explaining first that their ministry is essentially one of preaching and was commanded to them by Christ, therefore they would not leave it and be occupied with the ministry of distribution.

6.2.0.en: Look out among you: an application of the democratic system, so that the people feel their freedom, responsibility and participation in the organization of the Church, and consequently do not murmur afterward, because it was they who chose those responsible for distributing the gifts to them.

6.2.1.en: Seven men: a number sufficient for this ministry, and one of the sacred numbers that signify the work of the Holy Spirit, such as the seven sacraments of the Church.

6.2.2.en: Of honest report: known for uprightness and justice.

6.2.3.en: Full of the Holy Ghost: this appears in their devout life and their righteousness.

6.2.5.en: We may appoint: by prayer and the laying on of the Apostles' hands upon them.

6.2.6.en: This business: the distribution of gifts to the needy among the members of the Church.

6.2.7.en: The Apostles asked the people to choose seven to be set apart for this ministry, in whom certain conditions are met, namely being full of the Holy Spirit and of service.

6.2.8.en: Then the Church, that is, the Apostles, played their part in ordaining them and consecrating them to the ministry of distribution. Thus the procedure was in spirituality, democracy and wisdom.

6.3.0.en: The Apostles devote themselves to leading the corporate prayers and to preaching.

6.4.0.en: The saying pleased: the members of the Church were pleased with the counsel of the Apostles to choose seven to arrange and organize the material distribution in the Church.

6.4.1.en: All agreed on this and chose the seven, the first of whom was Stephen. Stephen: he was distinguished in his righteousness, and became the first martyr of Christianity (ch. 7:60). Philip: he is the one who preached in Samaria and baptized the Ethiopian eunuch (ch. 8:26-39), and afterward preached in Caesarea, and he had four virgin daughters who prophesied (ch. 21:8). Nicolas: who was not of Jewish origin, but a proselyte from Antioch, and who afterward became the founder of the heresy mentioned in the Book of Revelation (Rev 2:15).

6.5.0.en: The prayers of ordination were carried out with the laying on of hands, which the Church took as an ancient tradition for the transmission of priestly authority.

6.5.1.en: Here is a clear proclamation of the sacrament of the priesthood in the ordination of one of the ranks of the priesthood, which is the diaconate, and it has continued in the Church ever since in the ordination of the three degrees of the priesthood, the episcopate, the presbyterate and the diaconate, by the laying on of the bishops' hands on those who come forward for this service.

6.6.0.en: The word of God increased: the spread of the preaching of Christ.

6.6.1.en: The Church passed through the problem, and the number of believers in Jerusalem increased until it included for the first time a company of the Jewish priests, who were perhaps deeply affected by the tearing of the veil of the Temple on the day of the Crucifixion of Christ and felt the end of worship in the Temple, and who lost their position and their source of livelihood for their faith in Christ, whom they felt to be better than everything.

6.7.0.en: Because of Stephen's strong faith, in addition to his ministry in distributing gifts he helped the Apostles in preaching and teaching, and God strengthened him by working miracles, which drew many to faith.

6.7.1.en: Do not be disturbed if problems face you, and trust that the Holy Spirit is able to solve them. Take refuge in God in prayer, and rely on the guidance of your father of confession and the spiritual fathers, and think in a positive way, and God will solve all your problems.

6.8.0.en: Satan and the leaders of the Jews stirred up the members of some synagogues in Jerusalem, in which at this time there were many synagogues for preaching. Each group of the Jews living in foreign countries had synagogues in which they attended when they visited Jerusalem at the feasts and on pilgrimages, and this synagogue was one of them. The Libertines: Jews who had been captured in Rome as slaves and were then given their freedom by the Romans. The Cyrenians: from North Africa (Libya). The Alexandrians: that is, the Jews of Alexandria, whose number at that time reached about a million. Those of Cilicia: in Turkey, lying between Tarsus, the city of Saul (later Paul), and Asia, that is, western Turkey.

6.8.1.en: These began to dispute with Stephen, but they were not able to resist the wisdom of the Holy Spirit speaking on his tongue, and the evidence and proofs he presented from the books of the Old Testament.

6.9.0.en: They suborned men: they agreed with some Jews on false testimony against Stephen, and went in among those present in the synagogue and stirred them up and incited them against him.

6.9.1.en: Moses: against the Law of Moses, because he taught that these were types of the law of the New Testament.

6.9.2.en: God: because he taught that Christ is God, so they considered that blasphemy.

6.9.3.en: These Jews, as their leaders had earlier at the trial of Christ, resorted to intrigue and falsification through some of their men who had attended Stephen's sermons, and claimed that he was blaspheming Moses and God.

6.10.0.en: They stirred up the people: the group of Jews in revolt against Stephen disturbed and agitated the people, whether those gathered in the synagogue or those they visited in their homes.

6.10.1.en: The elders: the members of the Sanhedrin.

6.10.2.en: The scribes: those responsible for copying the books of the Old Testament, who were among the leaders of the people. The council: the Sanhedrin or council of the seventy elders, responsible for issuing decisions and judging the accused in religious matters.

6.10.3.en: They continued in their plan to stir up the people against him, as did the leaders of the Jews and the scribes, who in turn seized Stephen to be tried for that before the Sanhedrin.

6.11.0.en: Ceaseth not: continuing in teachings against the Jewish law.

6.11.1.en: This holy place: the Sanhedrin was meeting in one of the porches of the Temple, and what is meant by the place is the Jewish Temple.

6.11.2.en: Here false witnesses came forward testifying to Stephen's repeated offense against the dignity of the Temple and the Mosaic Law.

6.12.0.en: The witnesses said they had heard him themselves say that the Lord Christ, whom they called the Nazarene in order to disparage Him, because nothing good comes out of Nazareth (Jn 1:46), as they said in their proverbs, would destroy the Temple and change its rites, as they had said at the trial of Christ.

6.13.0.en: At the beginning of the trial, Stephen was calm in his features, his face shining, without fear or pride or fanaticism, like an angel.

6.13.1.en: Truly God appears in the conduct of His children and on their features, and this is a measure of God's dwelling in our hearts, for a joyful heart makes a cheerful countenance (Prov 15:13). So repeat inwardly prayers and psalms that give you an inner calm that shows on your features, and you will be a silent proclamation to everyone who sees you. Stephen's defense and stoning

7.0.s.en: (1) From Abraham to his father Moses

7.0.0.en: The trial of Stephen was about seven years after the Ascension of Christ, and the high priest asked Stephen to defend himself against the charge of blasphemy against Moses, God and the Temple, with which they had accused him.

7.1.0.en: Haran: a city lying west of the Euphrates in Iraq, north of Ur of the Chaldees.

7.1.1.en: The land that I shall show you: he means the land of Canaan, which is the region of the Jordan and Palestine, and He did not name it in order to test Abraham's reliance and obedience.

7.1.2.en: Stephen began with a preaching address, and the remarkable thing is that he did not defend himself at all, but set about a preaching effort toward the Jews, recounting their history to them to win them to his side, so that he could persuade them to believe in Christ. Despite their ill intentions toward him, Stephen addressed them with the utmost respect and called them brethren and fathers. During his address Stephen was showing them that God has many holy places in the world besides the Jewish Temple, whose destruction they considered blasphemy; so he told them that God appeared to Abraham between the Tigris and the Euphrates in his town, Ur of the Chaldees, to call him, and did not appear to him in Jerusalem.

7.2.0.en: The land of the Chaldeans: the city of Ur of the Chaldees.

7.2.1.en: This land, wherein you now dwell: Canaan.

7.2.2.en: Our father Abraham responded to the call of God, but his father Terah held on to him and went out with him, so he obeyed him and settled in Haran until Terah died, and God appeared to Abraham a second time and called him to the land of Canaan, and he obeyed.

7.3.0.en: God promised that the land would belong to the seed of Abraham, who in his lifetime did not possess any of it, and Abraham had no children at the time of the promise.

7.4.0.en: He informed him that his seed would be strangers in Egypt for about four hundred years, in many insults and troubles; and that was fulfilled.

7.5.0.en: God judges Pharaoh and the Egyptians for their wickedness. Then the sons of Abraham come out and worship God in the land of Canaan and not in Jerusalem, which they regarded as the summit of holiness.

7.6.0.en: Circumcision was the sign of the covenant between God and Abraham and his seed, and Abraham performed circumcision on Isaac on the eighth day from his birth as God commanded, an indication of the connection of the promise with eternal life, symbolized by the number "8" in the Holy Bible, because it comes after "7," the symbol of the time of the creation of the world.

7.6.1.en: Then came Jacob and the heads of the tribes, who envied Joseph their brother and sold him to Egypt, and that is a symbol of their envy of Christ and their selling Him to the Romans to kill Him, but God was with him.

7.7.0.en: God rescued Joseph from Potiphar's wife and from prison, and blessed him until he stood before the king of Egypt, who made him his first minister, responsible for the care and administration of all Egypt. By this Joseph is a type of Christ, who chose suffering and died for us and then rose to be the shepherd and head of the Church and of all His people.

7.8.0.en: Food: for them and for their cattle.

7.8.1.en: Our fathers: ten of his sons, namely those other than Joseph and Benjamin.

7.8.2.en: The first time: as in (Gen 45:4). When the famine began in Egypt and extended to Canaan and the whole world, hunger and distress reached the heads of the tribes also, so their father Jacob sent them to Egypt to get wheat.

7.9.0.en: Then he sent them a second time (Gen 45:16), when Joseph made himself known to them and Pharaoh learned of the whole family of Joseph.

7.10.0.en: Joseph sent and summoned his father and all his brothers and their families to Egypt, and their total number was about 75 souls.

7.11.0.en: Jacob and his sons lived in Egypt until they died there, and likewise Joseph.

7.12.0.en: When the people went out of Egypt they took the bones of their fathers, the heads of the tribes, and buried some of them in the cave of the field that Abraham bought from the sons of Heth, in which he was buried with Sarah and his son Isaac, and others in the tomb that Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor in Shechem in Samaria, and with them were the bones of Joseph also.

7.12.1.en: Stephen combined the two places bought by Abraham and Jacob, which are the two fields bought from the sons of Heth and from the sons of Hamor at Shechem in Samaria, so he said the field that Abraham bought in Shechem, meaning the two fields.

7.13.0.en: The time of the promise: the time of the fulfillment of God's promise to bring His people out of Egypt.

7.13.1.en: Which knew not Joseph: he did not appreciate the kindness and services of Joseph to Egypt.

7.13.2.en: Dealt subtilly: by trying to kill the males of the children of Israel by means of the two midwives, and then by casting them into the Nile, so that the people of God would grow weak.

7.13.3.en: Cast out: rejected from life by being killed after their birth.

7.13.4.en: The people of Israel were increasing greatly in number in Egypt, so that one of the kings who ruled after Joseph (most likely Rameses II, who was not a contemporary of Joseph but of course had heard of his story) tried by various means and wicked devices to do away with the Jews of Egypt by killing their male children as soon as they were born, so that they would die out.

7.13.5.en: Truly Satan fights the Church and tries to end its seed, but God always rescues His people at the right time. So do not be troubled by the agitation of the wicked, however strong they may seem, because God Himself protects you, and His blessing to you even increases in the days of distress and persecution.

7.14.0.en: At which time: the time of the royal command to cast the Jewish male children into the river Nile as soon as they were born.

7.14.2.en: Moses the prophet was born in 1571 BC, and his parents kept him three months in their house, thereby disobeying the king's command, out of their love for him and his beauty.

7.15.0.en: His parents were afterward forced to cast him into the Nile, but God arranged that one of the daughters of Pharaoh of Egypt, who had no children, should draw him out, and she adopted him as her son and raised him in the royal palace.

7.16.0.en: Moses grew up in the royal palace, learning the highest sciences of Egypt, which was famous at that time for learning and philosophy, so he became advanced in knowledge and distinguished in his conduct and works.

7.17.0.en: When Moses reached the age of forty, God put it in his mind to take care of his brethren the Jews, to visit them and ask after them, because the Egyptians, among whom Moses was counted as one, did not mingle with the Jews.

7.18.0.en: Moses saw an Egyptian wronging a Jew, so he tried to defend the Jew and remove the wrong from him, and killed the Egyptian, and he thought that the Jews would appreciate his mission to rescue them from the wrong of the Egyptians, but they rejected him when he tried to settle the quarrel between two of them, and the wrongdoer pushed him away, saying, who has set you up with authority over us?

7.18.1.en: This is a type of what the Jews did to the Lord Christ, for they did not understand that He was the Savior, but objected to Him, saying through their rulers, "By what authority doest thou these things?" (Mt 21:23).

7.19.0.en: The Jews reproached Moses and accused him of being a murderer, and thereby they could hand him over to Pharaoh to take vengeance on him and kill him. Likewise the Jews reproached Christ and insulted Him.

7.20.0.en: Moses fled from all of Egypt, and went to where the sons of Abraham by Keturah (the Midianites) were living, east of the Gulf of Aqaba, and there he married and had two sons, Gershom and Eliezer.

7.21.0.en: Moses lived there another forty years, until God appeared to him in the form of an angel in the flame of the bush in the wilderness, which was burning and was not consumed.

7.22.0.en: A voice: God did not appear in any form, but His voice was speaking from the burning bush.

7.22.1.en: Moses marveled at the sight and drew near to examine it, and God addressed him, saying:

7.22.2.en: I am the God of your fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so that Moses would understand that God is a lover of mankind to the degree that He calls Himself their God and rejoices in that, and because He would fulfill His promises to them by freeing them from the bondage of Egypt. So Moses was afraid and hid his eyes from the majesty of God.

7.23.0.en: God asked him to take off his shoes (as the priests later came to do during their ministry in the Jewish Temple, and as we do now in the church because its ground is holy ground). Thus Stephen indicated that there are holy grounds outside the Temple and Jerusalem, against which they accused him of blasphemy. The Temple is holy, and God also sanctified other places such as the one where He appeared to Moses in the bush, and Christ sanctifies in the New Testament many places such as the churches.

7.24.0.en: The affliction of my people: the pains of slavery and forced labor in Egypt.

7.24.1.en: Their groaning: their suffering and crying out to God to save them.

7.24.2.en: I am come down to deliver them: an expression according to human understanding to show that He will save them.

7.24.3.en: God declared that He would come to Egypt to rescue His people from Pharaoh, because He had heard their prayer and answered it, and He asked Moses to go to Egypt.

7.24.4.en: God's coming down to Egypt is a symbol of His Incarnation, in order to bind Satan by His cross and redeem us.

7.25.0.en: By the hand of the angel: God presents Himself in the form of an angel so that men can bear to speak with Him, but it is clear from the voice that came from the bush that it was the speech of God Himself.

7.25.1.en: Stephen returns to assure them that they, that is, their forefathers, resisted Moses in his saving ministry although God had sent him as a ruler, just as He later sent His Son as Ruler and Savior, yet they rejected Him. Likewise the Coptic Church still joins the Incarnation with the story of the bush in the hymns and praises of the month of Kiahk.

7.26.0.en: In the land of Egypt: that is, the ten plagues.

7.26.1.en: In the Red Sea: when he divided it with the rod, and it is also called Yam Suph. It was called the Red Sea because of the red weeds in it and the red sands and mountains beside it.

7.26.2.en: In the wilderness: such as the coming down of the manna and the quails.

7.26.3.en: Moses accomplished the mission in spite of that, as the Son accomplished salvation, and brought them out of the bondage of Pharaoh, working the ten wonderful plagues and many miracles and signs, that is, the marks that confirm he was sent from God (Ex 4:1-9), and he divided the Red Sea and led them on the wilderness journey to the border of the Promised Land for another forty years.

7.27.0.en: Stephen pointed to the prophecy of Moses in the Book of Deuteronomy (Deut 18:15-18) about Christ the Savior who would come sent from God from among the Jewish people, and Moses charged them to listen to Him, but they did not listen to Him, and resisted Him as they did Moses himself.

7.28.0.en: The church in the wilderness: he means the assembly of God with His people in the wilderness under the leadership of Moses and Aaron.

7.28.1.en: This is the Moses who led them by the power of the angel of the bush (God the Word) on the wilderness journey, and to whom He spoke on Mount Sinai and all along the journey, giving him life-giving words and commandments to deliver to them.

7.29.0.en: The Jews refused to obey him, but wanted to put him aside and return to Egypt, to which they were attached although they had come out of it.

7.30.0.en: The children of Israel asked Aaron to make them idols to worship, and refused to let the Lord go before them in the pillar of fire or cloud, preferring the idols to God, claiming that Moses had been lost on the mountain while he was receiving the two tablets of the covenant.

7.31.0.en: They made a calf: Aaron made from the gold that the Jews gave him an image of a calf, as the Egyptians used to worship the calf Apis.

7.31.1.en: The works of their own hands: because many shared in making the calf and organizing festivals and worship for it.

7.32.0.en: Gave them up: He abandoned them, so they went astray and worshiped created things, perhaps that they might return when they grew tired of their error.

7.32.1.en: The book of the prophets: the Jews gathered the books of the prophets into one book which they called the Book of the Prophets. Have ye offered: a rhetorical question meaning that they did not offer worship to God only but to idols also. The Lord was angry and delivered them to their enemies because they worshiped the stars and idols, as the prophet Amos prophesied in his prophecy (Amos 5:25-26), declaring their worship of idols throughout the wilderness journey.

7.33.0.en: Although the Tent of Meeting existed for the worship of God, they also carried with them small shrines containing an image of an idol named Moloch, easy to carry on the journey for worshiping the idol, and they worshiped another idol in the form of a star named Saturn (Remphan). This Moloch is the god of the sons of Ammon (the descendants of Lot), for whom Solomon the son of David built a shrine (1 Kgs 11:7) when he went astray from the worship of God because of his idolatrous wives, and he had a bronze image which they heated by lighting a fire under its outstretched arms, and then they offered their children to it as an offering by placing them on these two arms to be burned as a sacrifice to the idol, so God was angry and decreed their captivity to Babylon.

7.33.1.en: God does great miracles for us, yet we still resist Him as those did?! May we contemplate God's gifts and blessings in our lives, that we may thank Him every day and obey His commandments.

7.34.0.en: The Tent of Meeting contained the ark with the two tablets of the testimony inside it (on which the Ten Commandments were written), so it came to be called the tabernacle of witness, and Moses made it according to the pattern that the Lord showed him on the mountain.

7.35.0.en: Brought in: into the Promised Land.

7.35.1.en: Succeeded to: the sons held to it after the fathers, and inherited the worship of God through it. The possession of the Gentiles: in the Promised Land, where the children of Israel took possession in place of the peoples who had lived in these places.

7.35.2.en: The Jews took this tent by inheritance from the generation of Moses to the generation of Joshua and afterward, when they entered the Promised Land, which belonged to the Gentiles whom God drove out before the Jews, until the days of David.

7.36.0.en: Desired to find a tabernacle: he wanted to build a permanent house for God in place of the portable tent, and prepared the building materials.

7.36.1.en: Solomon built Him: God refused to let David build the house, because he had been in many wars and killed many, so He allowed his son, who lived in a time of peace, to build the Temple, in which they took great pride.

7.37.0.en: Dwelleth not: His presence is not confined to the Temple.

7.37.1.en: The prophet: Isaiah (Isa 66:1-2). God declared that He does not dwell in a building but first in the hearts of His children who believe in Him (Rom 8:11).

7.38.0.en: Heaven and earth cannot contain Him, so He does not rest in any house, however magnificent, but in the hearts of His children, because He is the maker of all houses and all their costly materials.

7.39.0.en: Here Stephen changed his style from the preceding historical presentation to rebuking his hearers, perhaps because he felt their distress at his words, which showed on their faces, so he was compelled to confront them quickly so that they would repent before they interrupted him and refused to hear the rest of his words; so he declared to them the hardness of their hearts, which had accompanied them throughout their history, so that their worship and their circumcision were outward and apparent only, and did not touch their hearts or their ears so that they would listen to Christ, and they lived resisting the voice of the Holy Spirit like their fathers.

7.40.0.en: The Jews rejected the witness of the Holy Spirit about Christ in the prophecies of the prophets of the Old Testament, and even killed the prophets and persecuted them, as Christ said in the parable of the vineyard (Lk 20:9-17), and they were the wicked husbandmen, trying to obliterate the prophecies the prophets had spoken about the incarnation of the Just One (Christ). And when He came they handed Him over to the Romans to kill Him, according to the counsel, opinion and suggestion of the Jews.

7.41.0.en: The Jews did not keep what they had received of the laws and commandments from Moses, to whom God delivered these commandments on the holy mountain by the hands of angels.

7.41.1.en: So man loses every blessing when he refuses to obey the Holy Bible delivered to him by God and continues in his error according to the evil of his thoughts. So accept the word of God that you read every day as a personal message to you, and apply it in your life.

7.41.2.en: (43) The martyrdom of Stephen (vv. 54-60), ch. 8:1 54 When they heard these things, they were enraged in their hearts, and they gnashed on him with their teeth. 55 But he, being full of the Holy Ghost, looked up steadfastly into heaven, and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God, 56 And said, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God." 57 Then they cried out with a loud voice, and stopped their ears, and ran upon him with one accord, 58 And cast him out of the city, and stoned him: and the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man's feet, whose name was Saul. 59 And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." 60 And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." And when he had said this, he fell asleep. Ch. 8:1 And Saul was consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the apostles.

7.42.0.en: Here their anger at Stephen reached its extreme because he had exposed the state of their wicked hearts, and their anger showed on their faces, so they gnashed their teeth because of their intense rage at him.

7.43.0.en: The right hand of God: that is, in the fullness of divine glory and majesty, for God has no right hand since He is unlimited.

7.43.1.en: After Stephen finished his sermon, and saw the wickedness of the Jews and their intentions to take vengeance on him, he felt that his mission had been completed, so he lifted his eyes toward heaven, beseeching God to support him, being filled with the Holy Spirit, and God showed him a comforting vision, for he saw heaven opened and the glory of God appearing in it, and the Lord Jesus standing in glory at the right hand of God to comfort and encourage him; and he declared to the hearers this great vision, which was the vision of Christ in His glory in heaven.

7.44.0.en: Here they did not wait for the council's verdict, but stopped their ears lest they hear from him what they counted as blasphemy, and with loud shouting they rushed upon him, proclaiming his blasphemy and his deserving death, and many accusations they were shouting.

7.45.0.en: They laid down their clothes: so that their hands might move freely for the stoning, and Saul of Tarsus kept their clothes until they had finished their task.

7.45.1.en: A young man: his age was between thirty and forty, because he was a member of the council, whose members could not be younger than thirty.

7.45.2.en: Saul: this is Saul of Tarsus who persecuted the Christians and later became the Apostle Paul. He was a member of the aforementioned synagogue that rose up against Stephen, because Tarsus is in the region of Cilicia.

7.45.3.en: They cast him out of Jerusalem lest he defile it, and stoned him with stones without a lawful verdict. The witnesses began the stoning according to the Law, that they might bear the consequence of their testimony if it was unjust.

7.46.0.en: While the Jews were stoning Stephen, he was calm, praying, asking God to receive his spirit to dwell with Him in heaven, and this shows the strength of his faith and his steadfastness in the last moments of his life.

7.47.0.en: Fell asleep: death is called sleep because it is a rest, for the spirit's transfer to God and its happiness with Him, and a rest for man from the toils of life.

7.47.1.en: Stephen knelt on his knees and prayed, asking forgiveness for those who stoned him, as his Lord Jesus Christ did on the Cross (Lk 23:34). Thus he ended his life with prayer, and his spirit was lifted up into the arms of Jesus Christ.

7.47.2.en: These feelings are the mark of Christians, for they love their enemies and ask God's forgiveness for them even while enduring the utmost torture from them.

7.47.3.en: Take care to complete your mission in life by witnessing for Christ and drawing those around you to Him, and whatever distress you endure, trust that Christ is beside you encouraging you and has prepared for you a great place in heaven. Ch. 8:1: St. Luke here declares that Saul of Tarsus was still persecuting the Christians up to this time, for he was among those who rose up against Stephen and condemned him to death. Persecution, dispersion and examples of preaching. This chapter is the beginning of the third part of the Book of Acts, which speaks of the persecution of the Church in Jerusalem, the dispersion that occurred and the appearance of the churches of the Gentiles.
